checkpoints.prompt: A route table contains `10.0.0.0/8` and `10.1.0.0/16`, and the destination is `10.1.2.3`. Which principle determines the route selected?

choices.text: The more specific `10.1.0.0/16` route takes precedence.
choices.explanation: In the same table, longest-prefix match selects the more specific route for the destination.

choices.text: Always select the route that was registered first.
choices.explanation: The deciding factor is how specifically the prefix matches the destination, not the registration order.

choices.text: Select based only on the target name, without checking the CIDR.
choices.explanation: The target is the next hop; it does not determine which destination matches.

choices.text: Always send traffic to both routes simultaneously.
choices.explanation: Ordinary route selection chooses the most specific match.

checkpoints.title: Routes determine the next hop for each destination.

checkpoints.prompt: Choose two components needed to allow only outbound requests from instances in a private subnet to an external API.

choices.text: Add a route from the private subnet’s route table to a NAT gateway.
choices.explanation: A NAT gateway supports outbound traffic from the private side.

choices.text: Provide a route from the NAT gateway to the internet.
choices.explanation: The NAT gateway needs a route on the public side to reach external destinations.

choices.text: Attach an IGW directly to the private instance.
choices.explanation: An IGW is used through a subnet route and public conditions; it does not directly replace the private-side egress design.

choices.text: Open all inbound ports for the external API.
choices.explanation: Allowing all inbound traffic is not required for outbound requests.

checkpoints.title: An IGW enables public reachability; a NAT gateway supports egress from the private side.

checkpoints.prompt: Which option allows return traffic for communication permitted by a security group (SG) without an explicit rule?

choices.text: a stateful security group
choices.explanation: An SG is stateful and handles return traffic for permitted communication based on connection state.

choices.text: only a stateless network ACL
choices.explanation: A network ACL (NACL) is a stateless filter that evaluates the return direction separately as well.

choices.text: route table
choices.explanation: A route table determines the next target and does not manage stateful permissions.

choices.text: DNS record
choices.explanation: A DNS record maps a name to a value and does not manage packet state.

checkpoints.title: Check subnet and instance permissions after routing traffic

checkpoints.prompt: The private service name resolves to the correct IP, and the destination SG already allows the traffic. Which combination should you check next to troubleshoot?

choices.text: Check the sender's route table and subnet ACL, along with the return path.
choices.explanation: Since the name and destination permissions are confirmed, investigate the outbound path and return path separately.

choices.text: Delete the DNS record and add a different name.
choices.explanation: Because the name resolves to the correct IP, changing the record is not the next troubleshooting step.

choices.text: Allow all traffic in the destination SG and skip checking the route.
choices.explanation: Traffic is already allowed, and opening everything would only reduce security.

choices.text: Always add a NAT gateway for private services, too.
choices.explanation: Adding a NAT gateway without checking the routing requirements for the private connection is inappropriate.

checkpoints.title: Troubleshoot private connections by checking names, routes, and permissions separately

choices.text: A route maps a destination CIDR or prefix list to a target.
choices.explanation: As described in the lesson, a route determines the next destination based on the address being routed.

choices.text: A route records only inbound Security Group ports.
choices.explanation: Security Groups and other filters control which ports are allowed; routes handle destinations and targets.

choices.text: A route always translates DNS names into public IP addresses.
choices.explanation: DNS translates names into IP addresses; that is not the role of a route table.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose one correct statement about VPC routes.
finalQuestions.title: Route configuration

choices.text: Check the route that includes 10.1.0.10 and its target in the source subnet.
choices.explanation: First, check whether the source has a route to the destination.

choices.text: Check whether the peer VPC has a return route to 10.0.2.0/24.
choices.explanation: The response must also be able to return to the source.

choices.text: If one side has a default route, do not check the route on the other side.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. With peering, both sides need routes to reach each other.

finalQuestions.prompt: You cannot connect from 10.0.2.0/24 to 10.1.0.10 over VPC peering. Choose one investigation step that is incorrect.
finalQuestions.title: Peering return route

choices.text: Without a return route on the peer side, a response may not make it back.
choices.explanation: Two-way communication also requires a route for the response.

choices.text: The route table must resolve DNS names.
choices.explanation: Name resolution is DNS’s responsibility; route tables handle IP destinations.

choices.text: If a route exists, NACLs and security groups are not evaluated.
choices.explanation: Routes and filters are separate control points, and both affect communication.

choices.text: The target may lack the necessary connection settings or reachability.
choices.explanation: Even if you select a target, the configuration may not provide a path to the destination.

choices.text: You must always delete the local route before checking external connectivity.
choices.explanation: The local route is retained for communication within the VPC; deleting it is not the right decision.

finalQuestions.prompt: Select the two correct reasons why having a route alone does not guarantee successful communication.
finalQuestions.title: Assessing reachability

choices.text: Configure the subnet’s route table with an outbound route to an IGW.
choices.explanation: An IGW is the target for routes to the internet.

choices.text: Assign a public IPv4 address or Elastic IP to the EC2 instance.
choices.explanation: A public IPv4 address or Elastic IP is required for IPv4 communication through an IGW.

choices.text: Placing a NAT gateway in the same private subnet makes an IGW unnecessary.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. A public NAT gateway is placed in a public subnet that has a route to an IGW.

choices.text: Allow the required traffic using security groups or similar controls.
choices.explanation: Traffic must be allowed by configuration separately from routing.

choices.text: Having only a private IPv4 address means the IGW automatically translates it for external access.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. External reachability over IPv4 requires a public IPv4 address or Elastic IP.

finalQuestions.prompt: Select the two statements that are incorrect conditions for making an EC2 instance reachable from the internet over IPv4.
finalQuestions.title: Conditions for external reachability

choices.text: Allow SSH to be initiated directly from outside to an EC2 instance in a private subnet.
choices.explanation: NAT provides an exit for traffic initiated from the private side; it is not intended for direct inbound connections.

choices.text: Provide an exit for an EC2 instance in a private subnet without a public IPv4 address to retrieve updates from outside.
choices.explanation: As in the lesson’s example of retrieving patches, it supports traffic initiated from the private side.

choices.text: Omit all Security Group rules in the VPC.
choices.explanation: NAT is not an authorization mechanism that replaces Security Groups or NACLs.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose one correct use of a NAT gateway.
finalQuestions.title: Purpose of NAT

choices.text: Check whether the private subnet’s default route targets the NAT gateway.
choices.explanation: A route from the source to the NAT gateway is required.

choices.text: Check whether the NAT gateway is Available.
choices.explanation: It cannot function as an egress point unless it is available.

choices.text: Check whether the NAT’s public subnet has a route to the IGW.
choices.explanation: The NAT itself must be able to reach the outside.

choices.text: Conclude that the NAT has failed if it cannot be pinged.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. NAT gateways do not respond to ping, so check their status, routes, and permissions.

finalQuestions.prompt: Patch retrieval from a private subnet has failed. Choose the one investigation step that is incorrect.
finalQuestions.title: Investigating the NAT route

choices.text: Security Groups are stateful and automatically allow return traffic for permitted connections.
choices.explanation: Security Groups track connection state.

choices.text: Network ACLs are stateful filters applied per instance.
choices.explanation: NACLs are stateless filters applied per subnet.

choices.text: Network ACLs allow inbound and outbound traffic separately for round-trip communication.
choices.explanation: Because they are stateless, return traffic must also be handled explicitly.

choices.text: Security Groups define only deny rules.
choices.explanation: Security Groups are a mechanism for defining allow rules.

choices.text: If a route exists, the NACL is not evaluated.
choices.explanation: Routes, NACLs, and Security Groups are evaluated at different layers.

finalQuestions.prompt: Select two correct statements about Security Groups and Network ACLs.
finalQuestions.title: How the filters differ

choices.text: Check return traffic in both inbound and outbound NACL rules.
choices.explanation: Because NACLs are stateless, rules are required in both directions.

choices.text: If the Security Group is stateful, no outbound NACL rule is needed.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. NACLs are evaluated independently of Security Groups.

choices.text: Allow HTTPS (port 443) from the ALB's Security Group in the EC2 Security Group.
choices.explanation: At the instance boundary, you can restrict the source to the ALB's Security Group.

choices.text: Since NACLs are associated only with EC2 instances, there is no need to check the ALB subnet.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. NACLs apply to subnets, so check both subnets along the route.

choices.text: Treat routes and filters as separate checkpoints.
choices.explanation: Routes determine the destination; filters determine whether traffic is allowed.

finalQuestions.prompt: HTTPS responses from the ALB to EC2 are not returning in a subnet that uses a NACL. Select the two incorrect judgments.
finalQuestions.title: NACL return traffic

choices.text: Open only the Security Group, and create a route if that fails.
choices.explanation: Before broadening permissions, you also need to check the path to the destination.

choices.text: Delete the NACL, then check the destination.
choices.explanation: Inspect the route and each filter in order without removing controls.

choices.text: Check the route, the NACL at the subnet boundary, and the Security Group at the instance boundary, in that order.
choices.explanation: This investigation follows the control points described in the lesson.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose the one correct order for investigating connectivity.
finalQuestions.title: Layer-by-layer checks

choices.text: Check whether the destination name resolves to the intended private IP.
choices.explanation: If the name returns a different IP, traffic will not follow the intended path.

choices.text: If DNS succeeds, there is no need to check routes or permissions.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Name resolution, reachability, and permissions are separate checkpoints.

choices.text: Check the route to the destination or the conditions for using the endpoint.
choices.explanation: Even after name resolution, the destination must actually be reachable.

finalQuestions.prompt: Choose the one incorrect troubleshooting step when you cannot connect to a private endpoint.
finalQuestions.title: Troubleshooting private connectivity

choices.text: Set routes to the peer VPC’s CIDR in the route tables of both VPCs.
choices.explanation: Creating a peering connection alone does not create routes from each subnet.

choices.text: The Security Groups and NACLs of both VPCs are automatically opened to all traffic.
choices.explanation: Allowed traffic rules are not changed automatically; define the required scope.

choices.text: DNS names always automatically return private IP addresses, so no verification is needed.
choices.explanation: Verify that the name resolution result points to the intended destination.

choices.text: No route is needed for return traffic.
choices.explanation: A return route is also required for two-way communication.

choices.text: Verify that the Security Group and NACL rules required for communication allow the traffic.
choices.explanation: Even when a route exists, the connection will fail if a filter denies the traffic.

finalQuestions.prompt: Select the two correct checks that are still required after creating a VPC peering connection.
finalQuestions.title: Checks after peering

choices.text: Check the return route on the peer side.
choices.explanation: Without a route for the response, the connection cannot be established.

choices.text: Because name resolution is correct, the filters must be allowing traffic.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. DNS and traffic permissions are separate layers.

choices.text: Check permissions along the path, such as NACLs and security groups.
choices.explanation: After confirming reachability, check the permissions at each boundary.

choices.text: Open all security groups to 0.0.0.0/0 and try again.
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. Maintain least privilege even while troubleshooting.

choices.text: If the configuration uses an endpoint policy on the destination, check whether the caller is permitted.
choices.explanation: An endpoint-specific policy can be the reason a request is denied.

finalQuestions.prompt: Name resolution returns a private IP, and the source route is also correct, but the connection still fails. Which two conclusions below are incorrect?
finalQuestions.title: Troubleshooting hypotheses

blocks.label: Summary
blocks.text: Troubleshoot communication failures by checking the destination, route, exposure scope, and filters in order.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Explain and investigate communication within and outside a VPC by distinguishing routes from control points.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Explain the role of a route based on its destination CIDR and target.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Distinguish the uses and requirements of an IGW and a NAT gateway.

blocks.label: Learning objective
blocks.text: Distinguish how security groups and network ACLs track connection state and where they apply.

blocks.label: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Trace the path of a private connection by checking the name, route, and permissions, in that order.

blocks.label: A route determines the next destination for each network destination
blocks.text: A VPC route table maps the destination CIDR of packets leaving a subnet to a target. Once the destination IP is known, the route that contains that IP is selected.

blocks.label: A route determines the next destination for each network destination
blocks.text: The local route keeps traffic for CIDRs within the VPC. When multiple routes in the same table match a destination IP, the longest prefix—that is, the most specific CIDR—is selected. For example, 10.1.2.3 matches both 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.0.0/16, so 10.1.0.0/16 is selected.

blocks.label: A route determines the next destination for each network destination
blocks.text: Do not decide by looking only at the default route; check the CIDR containment relationships.

steps.label: A route determines the next destination for each network destination

blocks.label: A route determines the next hop for each destination
blocks.text: Even if a route exists, that does not guarantee the target can reach the other end. Routes on the target side, VPN or peering configuration, and a return path are also required.

steps.label: A route determines the next hop for each destination

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: An EC2 instance in 10.0.2.0/24 cannot connect to 10.1.0.10.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Find the route containing destination 10.1.0.10 in the subnet’s table.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: If the target is peering, check whether the peer VPC also has a return route to 10.0.2.0/24.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: After checking the route, verify that communication is allowed on both sides.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can explain separately whether the destination, outbound path, or return path is missing.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: A 0.0.0.0/0 route means you can reach every private network.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: The target of a default route does not necessarily know how to reach that private network. You need a target for the destination and routes in both directions.

steps.label: This is incorrect and the correction

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A route is a pair consisting of a destination CIDR and a target.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Check reachability in both directions, including the return path.

blocks.label: IGW enables public reachability; NAT supports outbound traffic from the private side
blocks.text: An Internet Gateway (IGW) attaches to a VPC and serves as a target for internet-bound routes in a route table. An EC2 instance that must be reachable from outside over IPv4 needs a route to the IGW and a public IPv4 address or Elastic IP.

blocks.label: A NAT gateway is used when resources in a private subnet send outbound traffic to external destinations over IPv4. The NAT gateway itself is placed in a public subnet, which needs a route to the IGW.
blocks.text: IGW enables public reachability; NAT supports outbound traffic from the private side

steps.label: IGW enables public reachability; NAT supports outbound traffic from the private side

blocks.label: IGW enables public reachability; NAT supports outbound traffic from the private side
blocks.text: Placing a NAT in a private subnet alone does not provide an exit to the outside. Check the two steps: point the private subnet’s default route to the NAT, and the NAT’s subnet default route to the IGW.

blocks.label: IGW enables public reachability; NAT supports outbound traffic from the private side
blocks.text: Because pinging the NAT gateway’s own IP does not receive a response, do not conclude that there is a failure based only on a missing ping reply. Check its Available state, the two routes, and communication permissions.

steps.label: IGW enables public reachability; NAT supports outbound traffic from the private side

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: Allow only patch downloads from the private subnet; do not allow SSH access from the internet.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Place EC2 in a private subnet without a public IPv4 address.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Route 0.0.0.0/0 from the private subnet to a NAT gateway.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: Place the NAT gateway in a public subnet with an IGW route and a public IPv4 address.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: This allows connections initiated from EC2 while keeping them separate from direct inbound traffic through the IGW.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Creating a NAT gateway automatically gives a private subnet access to the internet.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Traffic cannot flow unless the private subnet has a route and the NAT side has an IGW route.

steps.label: This is incorrect and its correction

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: An IGW is a route target for public reachability.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: NAT is an egress point for IPv4 traffic initiated from the private side.

blocks.label: Check subnet and instance permissions after the route is in place
blocks.text: A Security Group is a stateful filter associated with an instance or network interface. Return traffic for an allowed connection is permitted automatically, so you generally allow only the required source and port.

blocks.label: Check subnet and instance permissions after the route is in place
blocks.text: A Network ACL is a stateless filter applied to a subnet. Because inbound and outbound traffic are evaluated separately, design both directions, including the ephemeral ports used for return traffic.

steps.label: Check subnet and instance permissions after the route is in place

blocks.label: Check the route first, then verify permissions at the subnet and instance levels
blocks.text: Routes, NACLs, and security groups are not interchangeable. A route determines the destination, a NACL controls the subnet boundary, and a security group controls the instance boundary, so check them in order along the traffic path.

steps.label: Check the route first, then verify permissions at the subnet and instance levels

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: HTTPS from the ALB to the Web EC2 instance is failing.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Confirm that the local route from the ALB subnet to the EC2 subnet remains in place.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: In the EC2 security group, allow traffic on port 443 from the ALB security group.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: When using a NACL, check the inbound and outbound rules required for the round trip.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can determine which direction to allow at which boundary, rather than simply opening a port.

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: If you allow port 443 in the Security Group, you don’t need an outbound rule in the NACL.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Because NACLs are stateless, return traffic must also be allowed separately.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Security Groups are stateful and apply at the instance level.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: NACLs are stateless and apply at the subnet level.

blocks.label: Troubleshoot private connectivity by checking names, routes, and permissions separately
blocks.text: When connecting to a private IP, first check the name resolution result. If the name returns an unintended public IP, checking the route or Security Group afterward will not lead to the intended private path.

blocks.label: Next, check whether the route in the source subnet sends the destination CIDR or prefix list to the correct target. VPC peering, Transit Gateway, VPN, and interface endpoints serve different purposes; simply connecting them does not provide automatic reachability to every CIDR.
blocks.text: Troubleshoot private connectivity by checking names, routes, and permissions separately

steps.label: Next, check whether the route in the source subnet sends the destination CIDR or prefix list to the correct target. VPC peering, Transit Gateway, VPN, and interface endpoints serve different purposes; simply connecting them does not provide automatic reachability to every CIDR.

blocks.label: Check names, routes, and permissions separately when troubleshooting private connectivity
blocks.text: Finally, check the NACL and Security Group, along with the return route on the other side. Fixing only one of DNS, routing, or authorization will not make communication succeed if another layer is missing.

steps.label: Check names, routes, and permissions separately when troubleshooting private connectivity

blocks.label: Scenario
blocks.text: The application cannot connect to the AWS service’s private endpoint.

blocks.label: Step 1
blocks.text: Check whether the destination name resolves to the endpoint’s private IP address.

blocks.label: Step 2
blocks.text: Check the route from the subnet to the endpoint or the endpoint’s usage requirements.

blocks.label: Step 3
blocks.text: If the configuration uses an endpoint policy or a Security Group, check whether the caller is permitted.

blocks.label: Conclusion
blocks.text: You can troubleshoot name resolution, reachability, and permissions in order without concluding that it is a “DNS failure.”

blocks.label: This is incorrect
blocks.text: Peering VPCs automatically permits all traffic between them.

blocks.label: Correction
blocks.text: Routes on both sides and permission at each boundary are required; Security Groups and NACLs do not open automatically.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Treat name resolution, routes, and permissions as separate checkpoints.

blocks.label: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Private connectivity still requires a return route and controls on the other side.
